utterances.text: Who did he tell you was in charge of the arming operation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked him what he knew about all that, on our way home. He said he knew about the arming operation and that he knew Mr. Danilo Veselinovic, who, as he put it, was the man number one in the arming of Serbs. He also said that he, Goran Zekic, had talked to Mr. Veselinovic about the arming of Serbs generally, and specifically in our area. He also mentioned the names of some other people who were involved: Mr. Tintor, and I can't recall the name of another man he mentioned now; I'll remember it later. So that was the conversation I had with Mr. Zekic on our way home.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say Mr. Tintor, are you referring to Jovan Tintor?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean Jovan Tintor, member of the Main Board at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned Danilo Veselinovic. Was he also a member of the Main Board at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he also was a member of the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you said that Mr. Dukic gave Mr. Zekic a piece of paper. Shortly thereafter, did you and Mr. Zekic travel someplace, and can you tell the Judges where you went in respect of the issue of arms?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not quite sure whether where you went is intended as a geographical question or as something more general, but if it's intended to be geographical, then there isn't much point in asking the witness: Did you and Mr. Zekic travel somewhere, and then: Can you tell the Judges where you went? Because the second bit of that question implies the answer to the first bit of the question. So they really need to be broken down to wait to see whether the answer to the first question is yes or no before the second question comes up at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if the answer to the first question would be no, no answer would be given to the second question any more. I do agree with you that these are two questions, but it's not inadmissible to combine them, I would say. Because if the first question would be answered by yes, then of course there's a -- I would say there's a natural need to answer the second question in order to provide information. If the answer to the first question would be no, then the Chamber would be surprised if an answer to the second question would be given.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that would be logical, but the point is the inherently leading nature of questions which are presented in that composite form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, it's leading in some extent, because the first question perhaps should have been: Did you ever meet Mr. Zekic at that time? And only then ask him whether you went somewhere with Mr. Zekic. But this is not leading to an extent that's not acceptable. So the objection is denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, you can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a little confused myself. The answer to the first question is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where did you go with Mr. Zekic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over the next few days, I went to Belgrade with Mr. Zekic, to see Mr. Mihalj Kertes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Please tell the Judges about that trip.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One morning, Goran Zekic came to collect me and said that I should get ready, that we were going to Belgrade. This was the late April. I think that was the time. I got ready and we left for Belgrade. On the way there, I said: "Where are we going?" And he didn't tell me right away what it was all about. I could just assume, based on the meeting in Milici, that this is what this was about. We came to Belgrade. Mr. Zekic is a -- used to study in Belgrade. He knows Belgrade very well. We came in front of the Serbian presidency building. That's where we parked the car. Goran Zekic announced us at the entrance. He said that we were there to see Mr. Kertes. I described where the building was, also the office, so I think there is no need for such details here. We went in. Mr. Kertes received us very quickly. We were brought in by a secretary. Mr. Kertes was alone in the office. He received us. We said that we had announced our visit earlier. Mr. Zekic did that, and Mr. Kertes knew what the visit was about. We sat down in the office and we began to discuss the topic for which we came.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you refer to Mr. Kertes, do you know his first name?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. His name is Mihalj Kertes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you please relate the conversation that you had with -- between you, Mr. Zekic, and Mr. Kertes.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my best recollection, we discussed the following: Zekic said that our visit was previously announced, and it was in connection with what was agreed earlier. He said that very discreetly, without mentioning weapons. Mr. Kertes said yes, that he knew about it, and then he continued the conversation on this topic, that he was in charge of that kind of business or those kinds of tasks, that he was carrying them out, arming the Serbs. He also mentioned Croatia and Kosovo and he related to us some details. One detail in connection with that job of his, he said that we should report to Bubanj Potok, in reference to this, this is a barracks or a warehouse, as far as I can recall, in Belgrade. Then we moved to a different topic, which was just an incidental topic. I don't remember exactly who asked Mr. Kertes what the political plans were of Serbia in connection with the region that we were in. I'm speaking about Podrinje. And then he said the sentence that I tried to quote as correctly as possible, that it was the position of Serbian politics that the left bank of the Drina would be exclusively Serb. He mentioned about 50 kilometres depth of territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's how I understood that remark of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, Mr. Kertes said that he was in charge of the provision of arms. I'd like to play an intercept for you. This intercept, Your Honours, is dated the 24th of June, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I remembered from intercepts played during the opening statement that it was almost impossible to follow the text in writing on the screen, so I do not know --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour, and I have prepared a translation in English and in B/C/S of the intercept. So it was hard for me as well to follow. It goes far too fast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just one minute. The technology is catching up with us again. If the registrar could mark the intercept itself, or give us a number for the intercept. I don't know what you need to mark, but I have something -- do you need this? I'll provide this to you shortly. If you could just give me the next number on that, and then give us numbers for the transcripts as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next number will be Prosecution number P46, for the intercept; and the transcripts will be P46A and P46A.1 for the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, the copies aren't here. Could I put -- have the English version placed on the ELMO, and I will -- we can pause during the playing of this intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, I think what we could do is we could play the intercept in its entirety through once. It's a short intercept. Mr. Deronjic could listen to it and then I could put the pages of the material, the translation on the ELMO thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So if we could just play the intercept in its entirety and then we'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, do you recognise one or both of those speakers by voice?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise the voice of Mr. Karadzic. I'm not sure about Mr. Kertes. I'm not sure that it's his voice. I only had the opportunity once to see him and hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, if we could -- let me ask you this, Mr. Deronjic. What does this -- in your opinion, what does this conversation deal with?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question really should be to his knowledge, not to his opinion. We've had quite a lot of questions this morning which are introduced with the phrase "in your view" and "in your opinion." That should, we suggest, be avoided if at all possible because it does have a tendency to steer the witness away from the proper ambit of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I respond, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This witness has listened to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Have you listened to this intercept before coming into Court today?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Having listened to this intercept, Mr. Deronjic, did you form an opinion as to what the content of this conversation related to?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I then ask if my learned friend thinks that's the appropriate way to ask the question, may I now seek the answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, as a matter of fact, I don't think that would be the appropriate way because that has exactly the same vice and exactly the same objection as the original question. The point isn't whether Mr. Deronjic has formed an opinion; after all, if he hasn't formed an opinion, he's presumably going to answer the question, if he answers it honestly, by saying to Mr. Harmon, "Well, I haven't got an opinion," and we move on to the next question. The vice in the question is he's being asked for an opinion at all, as opposed to what he knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But it's not always possible, Mr. Stewart, to distinguish exactly facts and opinion. If you would ask a witness whether a car was driving fast, that is, of course, opinion and fact mixed together. Mr. Deronjic, Mr. Harmon would like to know what this conversation, in view of you, was about. Because it always needs some interpretation. So therefore, you may answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make a suggestion, that in fact rather than preface the question with any reference to opinions or views, the simple question, what was the conversation about, with Your Honour's clear indication to the witness as to what primarily the Tribunal is looking for, would be preferable. It's the unnecessary introduction of the phrase "in your view" or "in your opinion." And we've had this more than once this morning. It's that unnecessary introduction of the phrase which is bound to have a tendency to steer the witness in the wrong direction towards opinion, as opposed to factual knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whenever questions can be put without this addition, Mr. Harmon, I think it would be appropriate to do so; on the other hand, it's not such an issue, because if it's really just facts that you could hear, that is, what is the third word spoken or what's the second part of the conversation, of course, if it's just facts, then of course the Chamber could, just by reading it, establish those same facts. For example, a telephone conversation would be about a football match, then we really do not need a witness to explain to us that the conversation is about a football match. So to that extent, facts that clearly come out from the conversation itself can be established by the Chamber. But if, on the basis of specific knowledge of a witness, he could add something to the meaning of that, I think he could explain that or ask the attention on certain aspects which the Chamber otherwise might not understand that well. That's, of course, the basis of his personal knowledge. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, what is this conversation about?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will just add one sentence. In the introduction. This conversation explicitly discusses the topic of furniture. It refers to 50 pieces of furniture a day. Then the logical question is asked: What is this? Is this furniture, or what is it? I would like to say that in my opinion, and according to the information that I have from that period, this is a conversation discussing the arms for Serbs, and that the expression, the term "furniture" is used to conceal the true intent to arm the people. Since I personally know that Mr. Kertes was involved in this business, this is a conclusion that I believe is justified, that what is being discussed here is the arming of Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and people who are helping in this endeavour, and people who are in a way 17 posing obstacles in this endeavour. This is my opinion, which allow may be 18 incorrect. Q. The intercept -- and if I could have the second page of the English version placed on the screen, on the ELMO. I'm sorry. The third page. If I can have the third page placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps in order -- I don't know what further questions you're going to put to the witness, Mr. Harmon, but I'd like to intervene with two questions. The first question, Mr. Deronjic, is: You explained more or less to us that "furniture" is a code word, at least doesn't mean furniture but means something else. Are you aware of any other occasion where the word "furniture" was used to refer to arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I'm not aware of such a case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Second question: Could you relate by your conversation with Mr. Kertes whether he professionally had anything to do with furniture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He didn't tell us anything, but I know that professionally he has nothing to do with furniture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From what you know what his profession was, you cannot relate that in any way to furniture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to one line in this conversation, and I'd like you to comment on it. This is attributed to Mihalj Kertes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is on the screen in front of you. It says, in response to Mr. Karadzic. Mr. Karadzic asked: "Does Slobo demand that he should decide about every business?" And Mr. Kertes answers: "No. Slobo has given Jovica and me carte blanche, but then he's Jovica's boss and he's driving Jovica crazy."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you comment on that line.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon. It is my assumption that the person being referred to here is Mr. Jovica Stanisic. If necessary, I can explain why I make this assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Slobo, who does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Undoubtedly, it refers to Mr. Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions in respect of this intercept. Let me go back to the conversation that you had with Mr. Kertes and Mr. Zekic in his office. Did he at some point in that conversation ask you if you wanted to pay a visit on Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what was your answer?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not wish to meet with Mr. Milosevic at that time, and we didn't know whether that was even possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned the conversation -- a statement that Mr. Kertes said about the left bank, and approximately 50 kilometres of the left bank being exclusively Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can I have the next exhibit, please, marked for identification and shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Given an exhibit number or marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number P47.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And could the B/C/S version be shown?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could the B/C/S version be presented to the witness. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, this exhibit -- are you familiar with this exhibit? Can you tell the Judges what this exhibit is.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this exhibit. It is a decision published in the Official Gazette of Republika Srpska. I think the date it was published is the 12th of May. I'm not sure of that, but it's definitely from the month of May. The actual decision is actually entitled: "Decision on strategic objectives of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And is there a name that is -- appears at the bottom of that particular decision?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's an assembly decision. Below it is the name of Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I'd like to focus your attention on strategic objective number 3?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if we could comment. Because although very strictly speaking it's a question which could wait until cross-examination, the simple fact is that this document says at the top that it's the Official Gazette of the Republika Srpska for Friday, the 26th of November, 1993. So when the witness says it's the decision published in the Official Gazette, and I think the date it was published is the 12th of May, it might just be helpful if the witness's attention could be directed to the contents of the document itself to see whether he is, in fact, happy with that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But could then perhaps also the attention of the witness be drawn to where the date of the 12th of May of 1992 appears in the document, so that he has a better reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. That's part of the same exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the other hand -- let me just first precisely check. Yes. Mr. Deronjic, you said it was published on the 12th of May. It says that -- I have some difficulties in reading, as a matter of fact, the publication exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can clarify this with the witness, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, in the lower left-hand corner of the decision itself, it has the date 12 May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And on the upper right-hand corner, near the words "Official Gazette of the Republika Srpska," it has 26 November 1993. Can you tell us what those dates represent, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the decision was adopted on the 12th of May, 1992 and that it was published in the Official Gazette in November 1993. I made a mistake, and I mixed up those two dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. In any event, we can proceed, Mr. Deronjic. I'd like to focus your attention on strategic objective number 3, which is, and I quote: "Establish a corridor in the Drina River Valley, that is, eliminate the Drina as a border separating Serbian states." And I would like you to comment on the statement made by Mr. Kertes in April of 1991 and this particular strategic objective which was promulgated on the 12th of May, 1992. Could you proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon. I think that these things are connected, that Mr. Kertes's statement, perhaps not in this form, refers to the strategic decision of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I would just like to add that I am familiar with one meeting devoted to this topic from the summer of 1991. This was a meeting in Bajina Basta, which is in Serbia, and it's a municipality bordering on the Srebrenica and Bratunac municipality. This was organised by intellectuals from Podrinje and from Belgrade. The meeting was entitled: "Drina, the backbone of the Serbian people." And I think that this topic, Drina, as not a border between Serbs, was something that was written about in the media in 1990 and 1991, and this is something that, in my opinion, is connected.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Deronjic, after leaving Mr. Kertes's office, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Goran Zekic and I went to Bubanj Potok, and there we were met by 20 an officer whose name I don't know, because I didn't ask. Mr. Zekic made his 21 acquaintance and went to the office, and I went inside those depots - those are indeed very large depots, storing arms of the Yugoslav People's Army - accompanied by a couple of soldiers. Mr. Zekic and the officer returned shortly, and Mr. Zekic and I reviewed for a while the arsenals in the depot. And Mr. Zekic told me that he had agreed a delivery for Bratunac and Srebrenica and that we could go home. On the way home, we talked a little about how to organise that first scheduled transport of arms for Bratunac and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did you discuss?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked about how to get those arms into Bosnia and Herzegovina, specifically to Bratunac and Srebrenica, but I, at least, didn't know how safe it was to drive those weapons through Serbia. So I asked Zekic what he knew about that aspect. He said that he would make arrangements for one truck to arrive in the neighbouring municipality of Ljubovija, whereas I was supposed to prepare a group of people from Bratunac to help us get those arms from Ljubovija into Bratunac and Srebrenica, a group of men whom I trusted implicitly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you give us some additional details about the specific arrangements as to who you trusted and what arrangements were made to store the arms in Bosnia itself.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I selected three men. Goran Zekic suggested some of them who were his friends. It so happened that some of them were presidents of the local boards in Bratunac. Mr. Slavko Jovanovic, Milan Sundjin, and Raso Milosevic, men from three different areas. It was agreed that Goran Zekic would let me know when the arms are arriving and that we should transport the weaponry to our localities and put them in safe storage and provide guards. That's what happened. The weapons arrived, and just by way of illustration, I said that the arms arrived when it was the finals of the football cup, and the Red Star football club became the champion of Europe. That's how I remember the date. That was the night when we got the arms across the Drina River. Goran Zekic went home to transport the arms further towards Srebrenica and put them in agreed depots, depots designated for people in the field. It was agreed that this should not be disclosed even to the closest associates, that we should keep it as secret as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And were these depots where the weapons were stored in Serbian-occupied areas?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What I heard in my earphones was Serbian occupation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No. Let me rephrase the question. Mr. Deronjic, where were these weapons stored in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arms depots in Bosnia were located in those Serb areas, that is, areas populated solely by Serbs. One was in Fakovici, near Drina River, another in Osansko, downstream, and the third --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter, they didn't hear the name of the third one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the name? The interpreters didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The third one was Kravica, a region populated solely by Serbs, located in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And once those weapons were put in storage, what happened to those weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing happened. This transport was effected in secret. But in the next period, in the summer, as far as I remember, there were already rumours about the arming operation in Bratunac. The secret was out, and pressure was brought to bear by some people who thought that they didn't receive arms, whereas some others did. So I issued orders to distribute those weapons to people who could be trusted to keep it secret. That was necessary, I thought, because there was a danger the police might find out about it and seize the weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask one question? I'm not that well aware of when what kind of championships, there are so many these days, are held, but could you give us a clear indication on how much time it took before the weapons were delivered, after your trip to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I don't know the exact date. It was the beginning of May. May 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May 1991. And your visit to Belgrade was in, from what I remember, early April of 1991; is that -- or just April? I have to check that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So a couple of weeks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even less, one could say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, in addition to this particular arms shipment that arrived at the beginning of May, did additional arms come to Bosnia and Herzegovina? Were there additional deliveries?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were other shipments. The process of arming Serbs in Bratunac continued and lasted up to the end of 1991. I indicated in my interview the sources from which I knew the weapons were shipped, and I also indicated those about which I had firsthand knowledge, although I was no longer directly involved. But I did attend a meeting together with Goran Zekic in the beginning of summer, in a place called Bajina Basta, a meeting with the president of the Executive Council of Bajina Basta, who told us that he was in charge for delivering arms to Srebrenica and Visegrad. Goran Zekic took me there to see if we in Bratunac could get some weapons from the Uzice Corps, and in a way, he managed to secure that. I had no longer any ties with Uzice after that, but Goran Zekic did manage to get a certain amount of weaponry over to Srebrenica. I indicated that we had another arms shipment from another source, and that is the JNA in Tuzla, where a garrison command was located. I have never been to Tuzla, but I heard from other people that Goran Zekic went there with Petar Jankovic, president of the municipal board of Kalesija, and they visited a general whose last name was also Kalesija [as interpreted]. With him, they agreed on arms shipment that were effected to Srebrenica. As far as I know, a part of it was left in Srebrenica. I know of another case of an arms delivery. It concerns an activity of the Territorial Defence, I believe, in August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you and just ask you: The record reads: " --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. The name of the general was Jankovic. He was the namesake of another Jankovic, Petar Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I'm referring, Your Honour, to the sentence that is at 12:13:54 -- it's page 63, and it is line 7, where the correction needs to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Deronjic, just to correct this record: You testified: "But I heard from other people that Goran Zekic went there and they visited a general whose last name was Kalesija." Is that spoken in error?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's an interpreter's error. I said that Goran Zekic and Mr. Jankovic, president of the municipal board from Kalesija, called on General Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did you tell us who Petar Jankovic was?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said Jankovic meaning Petar Jankovic, president of the SDS municipal board for Kalesija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did you know Petar Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, before I interrupted you, you were about to tell us another source by which the Bosnian Serbs acquired weapons. Could you continue with what you were going to say.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I know about one activity of the TO of Bratunac in the summer of 1991. How do I know about it? It was a coincidence. My brother-in-law, that is, the husband of my sister, was a professional instructor in the Territorial Defence for the areas of Bratunac and Srebrenica. I heard that he was holding drills involving some young men in the surroundings of Fakovici and I went together with a representative for that area for the SDS, where I found my brother-in-law and a large group of young men who were carrying out drills and training, to learn to handle weapons. I asked for an explanation, and my brother-in-law said it was on the orders of Mr. Sobot. The name is all I remember. And that was somebody from the staff of the Territorial Defence from Tuzla who was in charge of Bratunac and Srebrenica localities. This training was being carried out in that location, in that training centre. The place was called Ruljevici. It was also carried out in Kravica, in Banjevici, in a school building, in Podravanje, or Ravanje. All these are Serbian settlements. We discussed this because only Serbs were involved in the training. My brother-in-law explained that it was a good way for Serbs to arms themselves in that period, because it was well known that Muslims rejected involvement in all military activities, including those of the TO, whereas this exercise was part of the regular activities of the TO. In practice, however, it was exclusively training for Serbs. Another curious detail is that the arms delivered for the training of these people was left to them as their personal weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, when did the -- to your knowledge, when did the last shipment of arms arrive in the Bratunac municipality, and where did it arrive?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last delivery that I know of was to Kravica, when unrest broke out in Bratunac municipality as the result of the murder, the killing of two extremists in that time. I don't know how well these events are known, and if you have any questions, I'll be happy to answer them. And these weapons arrived from Serbia, across the Drina River, and were transported to that region by night, because the climate in the Bratunac municipality was already tainted by war and the town was full of barricades as a result of the killing of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I only wanted to ask you two small details. You mentioned the killing of two extremists. Were those people Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And was --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Bosnian Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is the town of Kravica adjacent to the town of Glogova?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see it's 12.20. I don't know if this is the appropriate time to break, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, this is approximately the time I had in mind. Could I ask the parties to review their agendas and to see whether, on the 17th of February, that is, next Tuesday, they would be willing to sit in the morning. In general, morning sessions are preferred by the parties to afternoon sessions, and there might be a possibility that we could sit in the morning. But of course I would not --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can give you my answer immediately, Your Honour. I prefer morning sessions and we would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would be available in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Our immediate answer, Your Honour, may we take a moment is in general we prefer morning sessions but that may not apply to that particular day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say it's not possible, then we have to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm not saying at this moment it's not possible. I'm just asking that we might think about it over the break at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. I hear then from you after the break. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But I could say, Your Honour, that in general, the Defence's preference is for morning sessions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's a generally felt preference, for morning activities, rather than late-evening activities. We'll adjourn until 20 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I inquire about the 17th of April. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Defence position is this: We -- it is quite a tall order. It is quite demanding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, let me be quite clear. If you say, for whatever reasons, because your son has his birthday or whatever, that it wouldn't suit you, I'm not going to change the programme on such short notice. That's it. So yes or no will do, and we'll -- Judges can change, Mr. Harmon can change to the morning. But if you have good reasons, that's enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I understand, and I'm very much appreciate what Your Honour is saying, effectively saying if we say no, we say no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In fact I was going to make another practical suggestion which may then help everybody, which is this, and it just starts from the simple position that it is very demanding for us to be ready to cross-examine Mr. Deronjic. There's no secret about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, if we -- if the Tribunal were to sit on Tuesday morning, but then we understand that one of the witnesses, Mr. Hasanovic, was not previously available, so he couldn't be brought in the contemplated order, but we understood I think from Mr. Hannis, but one of the Prosecution team, anyway, that Mr. Hasanovic could be available on the 18th, next Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I see Mr. Harmon is standing up. I don't know if he's going to correct a fact at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I don't want you to continue being misled. During the recess I just checked to see if this witness is available, has finally secured the necessary travel papers from the United States. I understand that he still has not done that, and therefore, Mr. Hasanovic may not be the next witness. The next witness may be Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's very easy then. With a great sort of respect, then, as far as Tuesday morning is concerned, Your Honour, the answer is a simple no, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll respect that. I mean, we -- it's -- the Chamber understands that such a decision by everyone prefers the morning session is not taken without some pain. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I inquire, Mr. President, what time we will conclude today's session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll continue until 45 minutes past 1.00, that's a quarter to 2.00. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Could I have the next exhibit, please, given a number for exhibit. And could Mr. Deronjic be provided with the B/C/S version of that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number P48.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, in front of you is Prosecutor's Exhibit 48. I would ask you: Have you seen this exhibit before?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon. I've seen it recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And when was the first time that you saw this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three or four days ago, when I met with you and when you showed me this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, prior to seeing this exhibit, you had provided the Office of the Prosecutor with a substantial amount of information in respect of the arming of the Bosnian Serbs in Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I supplied the information that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if you would inspect the first page of this exhibit, in the upper left-hand corner there is a name, the name of Petar Jankovic, with an address of Dubnica, and a telephone number. Do you know this individual?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's Petar Jankovic, president of the SDS municipal board of Dubnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Kalesija. Dubnica is a Serb-populated area in the municipality of Kalesija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have on the screen -- I'm sorry. Could I have Prosecutor's Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Again, rather than wait for tech -- just to orient Your Honours as to where Kalesija is, Your Honours can see from Prosecutor's Exhibit 35 the words "Bosnia and Herzegovina." Next to the end of Bosnia there's Sekovici, and if you go directly above that, you will see the municipality of Kalesija. This is just to orient Your Honours as to where Mr. Jankovic is from. Now if we could return to the exhibit that we were discussing, P48.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, did you have an opportunity to read through this particular exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Based on its contents and based on the name that appears on the front of this, who do you believe to be the author of this particular exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The author of this text is Petar Jankovic. That's his diary from that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now, after -- and just in general terms, after reviewing this particular diary, did you come to any conclusions, additional conclusions, in respect of the arming of the Bosnian Serbs in Eastern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And in general terms, because I'm going to direct you to specific parts of this diary, in general terms, what conclusions did you reach?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reached the conclusion that Petar Jankovic had been involved in the arming of the Serbs and that he carried out this arming in his own municipality and in neighbouring municipalities, mainly Lopari, the neighbouring municipality. And then there are other names of municipalities well known from that time. I wish to say that my thinking about this arming operation, and my conclusion, is that Mr. Petar Jankovic was not - and this is corroborated by this diary - a part of the group of people who were in charge of the arming operation. Instead, he established his own private connections for the purpose of arming Serbs in this region. This is attested by several segments of that diary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I would like to orient you through this diary, and I'm going to refer you to specific portions of it, Mr. Deronjic, and if you could refer to page 142 of the version in front of you. It bears the ERN number 00185071.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you read that? Mr. Deronjic, could you please read the entry that starts on the 29th of July, 1991. Do you see that portion of the diary entry in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On this page of the diary, dated the 29th of July, 1991, it says that Petar Jankovic called up Mr. Kerovic and that is Dr. Kerovic, from Lopari municipality. I believe he was a member of the Main Board of the SDS, telling him that they should go, as agreed, to Belgrade, to see Jovica. It says in brackets here "chief of state security." In my opinion, this is a reference to Jovica Stanisic, chief of Serbia's state security. At 12.00, they came to the office of Jovica Stanisic. I suppose that's him. And Jovica informs them of a fax sent by Jankovic, if I understand correctly, saying that 3.600 pieces of weapons were approved. The word used here is not "weapons," but I think that's meant. And also, a way of transportation is agreed. This is how I read this first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is -- the entry on this is July 29th, 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Let me refer you now to another segment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we please remain for one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The English text reads that he says that the weaponry has been approved, but less than 3.600, which we asked for. Your testimony with this text in front of you was that the 3.600 weapons were agreed, if I am not mistaken, were approved. I have some difficulties in reconciling your testimony and the text you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the term -- I didn't see it. I missed it. I'm just saying -- I'm trying to get used to the handwriting, even though I've read it before. But correctly, it says weapons were approved. That's what it says, in my text also. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, there's also some indication of the relative use of asking a witness to read a certain part, and if he misreads it, then we've just got the text as he sees it in front of him. I mean, I'm not going to stop you at this moment, but just be aware of that risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What I intend to do, Your Honour, is I intend to show him certain portions of this, have him read it to himself, have him comment on it and maybe take him to specific parts of it for his insights into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, I'd like to have you turn, please, to page 166 of the document in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I cannot see the page numbers on the document. Oh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have found it. I'm sorry. 160 and -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: 166, Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. We seem to be running into some practical difficulty here. I don't know whether it's us, but we have this document as supplied on a CD to us, and it only runs to 48 pages. I don't know what the explanation is, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll be glad to give the explanation. Mr. Deronjic has in front of him a handwritten copy of the diary, and I'm referring to the numbers that are on the pages of the B/C/S original version in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm referring as well, Your Honour, to a date that is referenced in each of these entries, because each entry has a date. I have an English translation of this diary. Mr. Stewart can check. Hopefully it will correspond to what he has on his disk. The page I'm referring to is page 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that's extremely helpful, Your Honour, because, after all, this is not supposed to be an IQ test. If I'm given page 40, then I can find it, but I can't work from the B/C/S, because I don't speak the language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That has been clarified. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, the entry --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, the entry that I'm asking you to read is on page 166. If you go back to -- quickly to page 164, you'll see the date of that entry is September 6th, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This page is actually at the beginning of this text, and I see that it is the 6th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, have you had a chance to read that diary entry?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some words I cannot decipher, but I have read the majority of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, can you provide the Judges with some insight as to this particular page of the diary?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can just say that I recognise some names. Mr. Jovica is mentioned. I assume that it refers to the same person, Jovica Stanisic. Mr. Kerovic is mentioned; I've already said who he is. Then there are papers mentioned, and some misunderstanding between Kerovic and Jankovic. I don't know exactly what this is about. It says here: It seems that" and then I cannot see this word, "to call the DB chief," this word behind, after, just after -- yes. I don't know what it says. Somebody is supposed to call the chief. "Kerovic says that he gave to Stanko Cvijan" - that man is completely unknown to me - "Radmilo looked at the papers." And that person from the other texts, from the other diary pages, I think, is, in my opinion, Mr. Radmilo Bogdanovic, who at that time was the minister of internal affairs in Serbia. But I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. There's a reference -- I'll quote a portion of this entry to you. It is at the end it says: "Before we left, Jovica said: 'Smallest number of people should be involved in this.' I say: 'No problems.'" What are your observations on that particular passage?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just allow me to find it. Is that at the end of this page? Are we still talking about 166 or is that at the end of the entire text?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's not at the end of the entire text, but it's toward the end of the text. There is a telephone number that Jovica gives at the telephone number and it's the entries shortly above that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I referred you, Mr. Deronjic, to the passage that says: "The smallest number of people should be involved." --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Any comments?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are conversations between the person providing the weapons to Petar Jankovic and is asking him that the fewest number of people is involved in this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now let me direct you, Mr. Deronjic, to the next passage in this diary, that is found on page 171.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Mr. Stewart, it's on page 41 of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I'm referring, Mr. Deronjic, to the entries for September the 8th, 1991, and September the 9th, 1991. Would you read the passage for September the 8th, 1991, and the first three lines of the entry for September the 9th, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first sentences, Petar Jankovic is supposed to go to bring some people who arrived in Borovo Selo -- from Borovo Selo. Borovo Selo is in Croatia. So based on that, I conclude that this was about people who went to Borovo Selo, where at the time there was fighting --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there. If you'd comment, please, Mr. Deronjic, if you've finished reading the passages I've directed you to, I'm interested in the passage that starts at the end of a number 1, 2, 3, it starts with: "Meeting at Vukosavci at 2000 hours" and that is found in the entry of September 8th, 1991. It's on page 171 of your text.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read that. 2000 hours, is meeting was held. I assume that this was in this village or this hamlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Without reading back to us what you see in front of you, Mr. Deronjic, I'd like you to read it, and then I will ask you to provide your comments to the Judges about what you've read, and I may ask you some specific questions about what's found in the text. So have you had a chance to read the passages to which I've directed you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you have any comments about these passages?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The implementation of some agreements regarding the arming of Serbs in that area, I'm not familiar with the names of these settlements. The agreement being made is about the distribution of the weapons. So I assume that this is about the implementation in the field of the arrangements made in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me direct you, Mr. Deronjic, to page 175 in the text before you. And I would like you to read over to and through the next page, 176 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I don't have either a date or a text, I'm hopelessly --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I haven't finished, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Kindly wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is found on page 42 of the English translation. The date of this is January 24th, 1992. And Mr. Deronjic, I would like you to read through the portion that says: "He promised to help to get weapons and we are working on that." When you've read through that text, let me know.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it. I've read up to that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. And what are your observations as to this portion of Mr. Jankovic's diary?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic notes in the diary that his activity is directed at General Jankovic. I mentioned that name. That was the commander of the Tuzla Corps, as far as I know. And he also met another man. His name is given here, but I don't know that man. I'd never heard of him. It says that he categorised him as a good Serb, and he says that he promised to help him about the weapons. This is obviously a military officer, and they are still working on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me direct --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- task.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- you further on that same date to the -- toward the end of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, it is found on page 43, the section I'm going to refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, if I can direct you to the portion that starts: "After the meeting in Zelina, Nikola called at 2300 to tell me I should call him at 0700." If you would read that. I can ... It starts at page 180, I believe, Mr. Deronjic, on your version.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At 2300, Nikola called.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If you'd read that passage to the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I make a practical suggestion, Mr. Harmon? We have at the front page, on the left part of the page, and this keeps from us from zooming out, and my eyes are becoming worse and worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We will assist, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I caused even a worse situation. Yes. That's what I like.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, can you provide the Court with your insights as to what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who Mr. Nikola is. This pertains to weapons for Petar Jankovic. The gentleman is introducing him to some military officer. I don't know that person either - and informs him when the weapons should arrive at Dubnica. That is the gist of this text. I don't know this other gentleman either, the one called Momcilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me refer, Mr. Deronjic, to page 184 of the version in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Mr. Stewart, it starts at page 43 of the version that you have. And this is a diary entry date of January the 25th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Mr. Deronjic, I would like to direct your attention to that part of the entry that starts with: "Meeting in Borogovo at 1600 hours." Do you see that portion of the text, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And I would like you to read to the end of the text, until it reads: "Everyone was pleased."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your comments, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Borogovo is. It's probably a village. Petar Jankovic is explaining to the people that -- he's explaining the agreement with the army, and every is satisfied or pleased with this agreement with the army. But I don't know what the actual agreement refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Let me direct your attention now, Mr. Deronjic, to an entry that is found on page 197 of your text.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, it's found on page 46 of the English translation and it is a diary entry of January 31st, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would like you to read that entry through the end of the sentence that says: "Flogging a dead horse."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your comments and observations, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic, at the Tuzla Corps command, meets Mr. Zekic. I think this is Goran Zekic. I'm sure of it, because I've already said that he knew Petar Jankovic and that he went to Tuzla with him, to the corps. And that a part of the weapons shipment should be given to Bratunac and Srebrenica, probably in accordance with an agreement between him and Zekic. I don't know who these other people are and what this SCA means, and I don't know who this Becir is. I don't know what that means, "tonight in Milici," I don't know what that means.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Let me refer you again to another portion of this diary. This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask one additional question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The text also reads: "You are not going to see the godfather." Is the godfather just what it means or did the word "godfather" have any specific meaning in that time in your circles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, there is no special meaning. I understand what you can be associated with, but I assume that "godfather" means General Jankovic. That would be the head of the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is your interpretation. Did you ever hear the word "godfather" used where you were sure that it was referring to Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petar Jankovic had several kums, best men. He also had a priest from Vlasenica who was his best man, and he would often refer to kum this and kum that. I heard from Petar Jankovic that his kum was also this other Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Have you one second for me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have another question for you. It reads, in English, and I have consulted with at least one of my -- of the other Judges, who is also not a native English speaker. It reads in English: "He gave me my share of ammo." But I don't know whether "ammo" is a word, a normal English word or whether it's an abbreviation or -- of course, I haven't seen the original B/C/S version, but could you perhaps check for me what it reads in B/C/S. So that's the -- just after Bratunac and Srebrenica mentioned, in English, it reads: "He gave me my share of ammo, out of which I should give some to ...."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the version in the Serbian language, which I have here, it says that -- it talks about "municija," ammunition, so this would be the cartridges or the bullets for weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what we guessed that it was, but it's now confirmed. Ammo, is that an ordinary abbreviation for ammunition?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it is, but it's a -- I don't know what it is in the American language, but in the English language it's, if you like, it's army slang and quite common slang, mild slang, nothing vulgar, but it sounds as if the correct translation here would simply have been "ammunition," and to introduce that slightly more colloquial slang connotation of the word was not a correct translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Judges apologise for not having been neither in the British or in the American army. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Neither were we, I think, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, finally let me turn your attention to page 201.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, page 47.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, I would like you to read two entries, one starting -- one dated February 4th, 1992. And if you would read the entry as well for February the 5th, 1992 to the end.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me -- Judge Orie asked you a question about kum. In the first sentence is a person identified as the godfather?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It's obvious that Mr. Jankovic has several kums. This is Dancic, this Dancic person in Tuzla is somebody I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we will provide evidence as to the identity of this individual later in the course of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll wait for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could I have your comments, please, on these two diary entries.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Jankovic wrote down that -- excuse me. I would just like to look it over. With Vesna, his wife, Mr. Jankovic met in Tuzla, with this kum, in a hotel, where he gave him a gift. They were at dinner, and he gave him a present. This is a briefcase or a pen, as far as I can see. Yes, a pen and a briefcase. This is probably about -- the conversation probably included mention of weapons and that there should be some kind of meeting with General Jankovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And have you read the entry --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Dated February 5th, 1992, the next entry that starts on page 204?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The same page, Mr. Stewart, page 47.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read this first part. This is a meeting with General Jankovic, in Tuzla. Mr. Petar Jankovic mentions some people whom I don't know. I don't know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And this -- well, it says the following, I'd like your comments, Mr. Deronjic. I'm referring to the entry of February 5th, 1992, the third sentence: "The general received us pleasantly. Just as we started presenting our requests, godfather arrived." And then I won't read the whole sentence. It goes on to say: "Requests are about providing the unit with weapons."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 450 pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And does this entry confirm what Mr. Zekic had informed you about the role of General Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that information about Zekic being in Tuzla was something that I did not hear from him. I heard it from his secretary in the party, Mr. Jokic, who showed me a pistol on one occasion, which was issued to him from the army. He showed me a receipt from some military officer in Tuzla. And then he told me that Zekic, Petar Jankovic were in Tuzla together. This is confirmed from this diary, the series of contacts that Petar Jankovic had with General Jankovic, and indicates that on one occasion, Mr. Goran Zekic also attended one of those meetings in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You mention a receipt that was given to Mr. Jokic. Let me show you the next exhibit, please, which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next number is Prosecution Exhibit number P49.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if I could have the B/C/S version of that exhibit put in front of Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, I direct your attention to the signature on the lower left-hand side of the document. Are you able to identify that signature?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the lower corner, it says "Major Jablanovic." No. Taken over Petar. "Taken over by Petar." I've never had occasion that I remember to see the signature of Petar Jankovic, so I couldn't swear that it is his signature. But the handwriting is very similar to the writing in the diary, which I believe to be Petar Jankovic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. And there appears, Mr. Deronjic, on the B/C/S copy before you, a stamp. What is that stamp?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the stamp of the military post box Tuzla, indicating also the number of that military post office, which means nothing to me, because I don't know how these post offices were numbered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And this appears to be, does it not, a receipt for a pistol and some bullets and a rap for pistol, that I'm unfamiliar with?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if we could show Mr. Deronjic the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number P50.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, I direct your attention to the bottom middle block on that document. Do you see a name?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see it. It says Petar Jankovic, and the signature is identical to the one on the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And this document is dated October the 28th, 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And it describes certain weapons and bullets; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So this -- does this appear to be a receipt for weapons of various types?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In my mind, these arms were received by Petar Jankovic, because it says "received by Petar Jankovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now if I could have the next exhibit marked, please, as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P51.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If the B/C/S version again could be placed before Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, take a moment to acquaint yourself with that document. Let me ask you: Have you seen this document before coming in to testify?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, on the first page of this document, let me just orient the Court. On the first page of this document, it is dated in the upper left-hand corner March the 20th, 1992. It is from the command of the 2nd Military District. It is a military secret, strictly confidential, and it is from General -- or the commander, General Kukanjac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If you could turn to the second page of the document in front of you. The title of this document is: "Conclusions of the evaluation of the situation on the BiH territory in the zone of responsibility of 2nd Military District," again, marked "military secret, strictly confidential."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would like to direct your attention, Mr. Deronjic, to a section of that document, that is, part 4. It says: "Paramilitary organisation in Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if I could refer you, Mr. Deronjic, to the paragraph directly above that.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: As soon as it comes on the screen. It looks like it's resisting. I will read this paragraph to you. Mr. Deronjic, this paragraph says -- and it relates to the preceding paragraph. It says: "Regarding this matter, commander of the 2nd Military District will soon have a discussion with the leadership of the Serbian people (Karadzic, Koljevic, Plavsic, Krajisnik, and Dukic)." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, if you'd turn, Mr. Deronjic, to part 5, which in your text --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Mr. Stewart, this is on -- if you have it on CD, it's on page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Part 5 starts with: Volunteer units in the zone of the 2nd Military District."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you read that text, Mr. Deronjic, through the second paragraph that says "some experiences ..."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you agree with me, Mr. Deronjic, that this paragraph relates to providing weapons to volunteer units that are not part of the JNA or Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- this is a reference to volunteer units --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me direct you to 5, subpart c, the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "For the time being, it would be necessary to stop with the formation and arming of volunteer units."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me read you -- do you see a 5, and then you see, lower-case letter, a, b, and c. I'd like to direct you to a certain portion. Do you that "c"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you read the last sentence of that.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It says: "Volunteer units are outside of the establishment composition of the army and TO." It is not very clearly legible, but I can distinguish that that is the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And the subpart b directly above that, discusses how many people there were, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 69.100-something men.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, go down, if you would, Mr. Deronjic, to subpart f?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I make two comments, please, Your Honour. One is that since the witness is here and we do have an apparently illegible passage in 5c it might be helpful if the witness were able to assist the Tribunal and everybody with that apparently illegible part at the very beginning of c. He may or may not, but he stands a better chance than the rest of us because it's his language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that the translation is also made by someone who knows the language. But could you read the very first words of subparagraph c.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I can't make out the first two words. The first two words are completely illegible. Then it says: "Is not envisaged for the replenishment of the RJ of the 2nd TO. All units in the 2nd Military District," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: By the way, of course, I agree if the translation wasn't made by somebody who is familiar with the language, we'd all be in trouble. But that "d" is just a very obvious misprint in the title, in the heading, to that number of people in the zone. It's clearly the number of people in the zone of the corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps could you read the title of d, of subparagraph d. Could you please read the title in your language. Aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Troop strength is 69.100." We can't make out the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- Referring to D, not to B, of Bernard, but to D of Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency. D: ", "Number of men in the zones of the corps."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I make a suggestion? Rather than having these kind of interruptions, I think counsel and I could agree out of the courtroom as to these kind of language difficulties and I would be able to proceed in a much more expeditious fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It could save time in Court, and let me make then the following observation: If it would be something that would really obstruct the understanding of the Chamber, it certainly should be done at the very moment. But, as a matter of fact, this correction perhaps we should have -- we would have overlooked it anyhow. We could be informed about it later that there's a -- that there's a translation which is not fully correct. So I would like to invite the parties to intervene and to interrupt whenever really necessary for our understanding and otherwise to arrange for the matters outside of Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that, it is a quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I had only a few more questions about this document, but I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then I first would have to know how much additional time would be available, in view of the afternoon session, because tapes have to be exchanged, et cetera. And also in respect of the interpreters and technicians. [Trial Chamber and registrar confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unfortunately, for practical and technical reasons, since this courtroom will be used and since there are a lot of technical aspects have to be dealt with first, I have to stop you at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, may I -- what I may have forgotten yesterday. May I instruct you not to speak with anyone. That means not with parties, not with other inmates, not with whomever, speak about your testimony that you have given in this Court and that you're still about to give in this Court. We'd like to see you back, then, next Monday. We are sitting in the morning on Monday in courtroom -- Madam Registrar? Courtroom I. We adjourn until Monday, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. Before Your Honour adjourns. Could I say: I accept the comment made about the corrections, the particular one about corps and corpses was perhaps slightly unfortunate which is why we mentioned that. But may we just inquire what the position is in relation to our application for certification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The only thing I can tell you that we have read your submission that is either filed or not on the basis --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It has been filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has been filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the basis of that document, the Chamber will not change its position as it has decided before. That means that -- I can tell you that perhaps the main reason for that, your submission repeats what risk, or in your view, serious risk there is that a testimony -- but perhaps I'll first ask Mr. Deronjic to be escorted out of the courtroom. Could you please escort Mr. Deronjic out of the courtroom. Mr. Cvijetic, I don't think your presence is necessary any more for what we are discussing at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I will be very brief, because we have to leave this courtroom. It's very much emphasised in your submission of this morning what risk of a untruthful testimony exists, and apart from that, specific attention is given to the procedural issues as we find them in the Rule - what is it? - 73. The Chamber doesn't change its position on the basis of this, because the Chamber in its decision has, in its oral decision, has explained clearly that it is aware that the situation has a risk that this could happen. But the Chamber also explained that that's not the definition of the situation as a whole. The Chamber has also explained that there are other mechanisms also in place which might lead in another direction, and the Chamber has also explained that if one waits, that there might again be other psychological mechanisms that could either favour or disfavour a truthful testimony. To that extent, this submission emphasises one part where the Chamber has sought to balance and to see what is the weight of each of these circumstances, each of these risks. On the basis of that, the Chamber has decided not to change its view at this moment, and our work this afternoon -- I hope to deliver a decision in writing, if possible, even this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: On the -- when Your Honour says "decision in writing," Your Honour means on the original motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which would give you an opportunity to further study the decision of the Chamber and to make any further submissions you would like to make on the basis of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I'm obliged, Your Honour. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have to adjourn because the courtroom is needed we'll adjourn for the second time until Monday morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
